shots.narration: Orcas kill great white sharks, moose and blue whales.
In the wild, they have no confirmed record of killing a single person.
Doug is going to find out why.
Snacks.
Chinook Salmon.
Off the coasts of Washington and British Columbia lives a family of orcas
that eats almost nothing but fish, and it has a favorite.
These orcas are called residents, and they are extremely picky eaters.
Here's the strange part.
A University of British Columbia study found that in six of the last forty years,
the southern residents simply didn't get enough to eat.
Harbor seals swim through the same waters,
and a different population of orcas eats them all the time.
Researchers have never confirmed a resident orca eating a seal.
They would rather go hungry than change the menu.
What they want is Chinook.
It is the biggest salmon in the Pacific, and a typical adult is about a meter long
and weighs around fourteen kilograms, roughly the weight of two bowling balls.
Researchers who followed these orcas for years found that they hunt Chinook on purpose,
while smaller salmon that far outnumber it mostly swim on by.
Canadian government scientists think the orcas favor it for its size, its fat
and the fact that it is around all year.
The southern residents are now endangered,
and United States government scientists name a shortage of Chinook as one of their main threats.
Orcas don't hunt people. They hunt salmon.
Which is exactly why Doug is dressed as one.
Doug waved at the pod, hoping to be ignored,
and he was not ignored.
Doug did not agree to this.
They took the salmon, and they had no particular opinion about Doug.
Sea Otter.
A sea otter spends much of its life floating on its back,
cracking shellfish open with a rock it keeps tucked under its arm.
It has the densest fur of any mammal, up to about a million hairs in a single square inch,
and a big male weighs around forty-five kilograms, roughly six bowling balls.
In the nineteen nineties, sea otters around Alaska's Aleutian Islands started to vanish.
Across large parts of western Alaska, their numbers fell by about a quarter every year.
In one bay on Adak Island, about three out of every four otters disappeared in four years.
But this is the odd part.
The team that studied it, led by the ecologist James Estes, proposed a suspect nobody expected.
Orcas.
Before nineteen ninety-one, the researchers had never seen orcas eating otters there,
and it took Estes about two years to become convinced.
Estes linked the change to a collapse in the orcas' usual prey, seals and sea lions,
and when that food ran short, it seems the orcas looked elsewhere.
Meanwhile, in a lagoon the orcas couldn't reach, the otters stayed perfectly stable.
So orcas will change the menu, when the ocean changes it for them.
Orcas here had started eating otters, so naturally, Doug is an otter.
He floated there, perfectly at peace, until a fin went by
and the rock was wearing the cap.
The researchers calculated that as few as four orcas eating nothing but otters
could explain the decline across an enormous stretch of coastline.
Doug-sized.
Harbor Seal.
From here, the animals on the menu are roughly the size of Doug,
and the orcas that hunt them are a different kind entirely.
An adult harbor seal can weigh up to about one hundred and thirty kilograms, nearly eighteen bowling balls,
and a small adult weighs about the same as Doug.
Sharing the coast with the salmon eaters are Bigg's orcas, and they hunt marine mammals.
In one long study off British Columbia, more than half of the attacks researchers saw were on harbor seals.
Seals have excellent underwater hearing and can pick up orca calls from kilometers away.
In playback experiments, harbor seals reacted strongly to the calls of mammal-eating orcas,
but ignored the familiar calls of the local fish eaters.
So the seal hunters mostly keep quiet.
Researchers found that they rarely call while hunting and save most of their noise for after a kill.
There is one human case worth knowing.
In nineteen seventy-two, an orca bit a surfer off Point Sur, California,
but it let go quickly, and he survived.
The researcher Erich Hoyt, who interviewed him, thought the whale may have mistaken him for a seal.
It's still described as the only fairly well-documented case of a wild orca biting a person,
and even then, the orca let go.
So it isn't that we're the wrong size.
Doug paddled out in the seal costume,
and an orca took the surfboard, considered it for a moment, and gave it back.
Doug is fine.
We had been very confident about this one, and the orca apparently had not.
Dolphin.
Dolphins are fast, social and clever,
which sounds like exactly the kind of animal that shouldn't end up on anyone's menu.
Technically, the orca is a dolphin, the largest member of the whole family.
It can grow to almost ten meters long
and weigh about ten tonnes, as much as five average new cars.
Pacific white-sided dolphins weigh up to about one hundred and eighty kilograms,
and they share the coast with Bigg's orcas.
Off British Columbia, orcas are the only predators known to kill them regularly.
Researchers who photographed more than four hundred of these dolphins
found healed orca scars about eight times more often than scars from fishing gear.
The attacks themselves are rarely seen.
Between nineteen seventy-three and nineteen ninety-six, only one kill was reported off British Columbia,
although fourteen more attacks were seen over the next fifteen years.
Dall's porpoises are possibly the fastest of all dolphins and porpoises.
So Bigg's orcas hunt them in bays, working together to block their escape into open water.
The unsettling part is this.
The largest dolphin in the ocean eats dolphins,
and in one long study, Bigg's orcas were seen taking six different species of marine mammal.
Being clever doesn't protect you, and neither does being family.
Doug swam up in the dolphin costume and greeted the orca as family,
but the orca did not see the resemblance.
Doug has died. Again.
Off British Columbia, roughly one in every twenty-five of the dolphins photographed was carrying orca scars.
Stingray.
You'd think a predator would skip any animal that comes with its own built-in weapon.
New Zealand's orcas don't.
They hunt rays in very shallow water, close to sandy beaches, including eagle rays and short-tail stingrays.
Elsewhere in the world, orcas eat fish, seals and dolphins,
but according to Te Ara, New Zealand's government encyclopedia,
these orcas are the only group known to eat rays as a staple food.
The short-tail stingray is one of the largest stingrays in the world.
It can measure about two point one meters across, wider than a standard door is tall,
and weigh up to three hundred and fifty kilograms.
Its tail carries a barbed spine, with venom held in grooves along it.
The worst part is what happened in nineteen ninety-eight.
A young female orca was found dead near the Noises Islands in the Hauraki Gulf.
At the necropsy, vets concluded she had probably been killed by a stingray spine.
The orcas kept hunting rays anyway,
even though hunting this close to shore is risky enough that New Zealand orcas sometimes strand themselves doing it.
Researchers have watched the same orcas get stuck, then work themselves free.
So it isn't that we're too dangerous to bother with.
Doug buried himself in the sand, with only his eyes and the cap showing, and waited.
Then the sand moved, and only the cap was showing.
The ray brings venom to the fight, and the orcas treat it as packaging.
Bigger.
Moose.
A moose is a land animal, which ought to keep it well away from anything that hunts at sea.
A big bull moose in Alaska can weigh up to about seven hundred and twenty-five kilograms,
more than a third of an average new car.
Moose are strong swimmers,
and along Alaska's coast they cross big stretches of water, between islands and across coves.
Researchers think part of the draw is water plants, which give moose the sodium they crave.
That is where it goes wrong.
In nineteen ninety-three, in Icy Strait in southeast Alaska,
two fishermen watched three or four orcas attack a pair of swimming moose.
The orcas killed one of them, and the other didn't survive either.
Two leading researchers of these orcas, John Ford and Graeme Ellis, describe it in their book on the mammal hunters.
An Alaska Department of Fish and Game spokesman described this kind of predation as rare, but documented.
He said the roving, mammal-hunting orcas were the likely culprits, not the local fish eaters.
Off Vancouver Island, orcas have also been seen circling a small rock where two deer had taken refuge.
So being a land animal stops counting the moment you get in the water.
Doug swam between two islands in the moose costume, looking more dignified than he ever has,
right up until the antlers floated on without him.
Two fishermen, one channel, and a moose that only wanted to reach the next island.
Great White Shark.
Ask most people to name the most dangerous animal in the sea, and this is the one they'll pick.
Adult great whites typically weigh between five hundred and twenty and seven hundred and seventy kilograms.
A big female can top a tonne, more than half the weight of an average new car.
Off South Africa, a pair of orcas known as Port and Starboard, named for their collapsed fins,
has been linked to killing great whites.
Every recorded kill there had involved two or more orcas.
Since orcas now eat great whites, Doug is, of course, a great white.
But here's the unbelievable part.
On the eighteenth of June, two thousand twenty-three, near Seal Island in Mossel Bay, Starboard did it on his own.
Researchers and tourists on two boats filmed him take a juvenile white shark about two and a half meters long,
in roughly two minutes.
It was the first recorded case of a single orca killing a great white.
There's an older trick as well, from nineteen ninety-seven,
when an orca off California's Farallon Islands was seen holding a white shark upside down for about fifteen minutes.
Flipping a shark over can put it into a trance-like state called tonic immobility, and that is likely what happened.
So a young great white, of the most feared species most people can name, lasted about two minutes against one orca.
An orca turned Doug upside down, and he went very still and stayed that way.
One orca, one shark, about two minutes, and Starboard didn't even need his partner.
Gray Whale Calf.
This is the first whale on the list, and whales are much harder to push around.
A newborn gray whale weighs about nine hundred kilograms, roughly half an average new car.

shots.narration: Its mother can weigh about forty tonnes, the same as twenty cars.
Gray whales make one of the longest migrations of any mammal, about sixteen thousand kilometers there and back.
Each spring, mothers and calves head north along the coast, and Bigg's orcas wait for them.
At Unimak Island in Alaska, researchers watched more than one hundred and fifty of these orcas gather during the migration.
Most attacks were on calves or yearlings, by small groups of three or four orcas.
Here's where the list changes.
The mothers fight back, and when they defended their young aggressively, the orcas broke off.
Sometimes, strangers turn up.
In May two thousand twelve, in Monterey Bay, California, orcas attacked a gray whale mother and her calf.
Two humpbacks were already there, and after the calf was killed, about fourteen more arrived.
For six and a half hours, they harassed the orcas anyway, slashing at them with flippers and tails.
A review of over a hundred encounters found that humpbacks often charge in to break up orca attacks,
even when the target is a completely different species.
Doug stayed close to a mother.
The orcas came, two humpbacks crashed in, and the orcas left.
We are slightly disappointed, and for completeness, have added Doug to the menu.

elements.text: GRAY WHALE CALF, 900 kg AT BIRTH

shots.narration: For the first time on this list, something made the orcas back off, and some of the help came from strangers.
Giants.
Whale Shark.
The whale shark is the biggest fish alive,
a slow, gentle filter feeder that cruises along swallowing plankton.
Adults can reach around eighteen meters, almost twice the length of the biggest orca.

elements.text: GRAY WHALE CALF, 900 kg AT BIRTH

shots.narration: The heaviest one ever scientifically recorded, caught off Pakistan in nineteen forty-nine,
weighed an estimated twenty-one and a half tonnes, more than two big orcas put together.
Between two thousand eighteen and two thousand twenty-four,
researchers documented four orca attacks on whale sharks in the southern Gulf of California,
using photos and video from scientists and members of the public.
One of the sharks was a juvenile about six meters long, three doors laid end to end.
The orcas worked as a team, striking the shark until it turned upside down.
The researchers point out that young whale sharks are more vulnerable to predators than adults are.
What makes this one different is who did it.
An adult male the researchers call Moctezuma appears in three of the four attacks.
A female seen with him before joined one of them.
The researchers suggest there may be a specialized group of shark hunters living in the region.
So a brand-new prey can end up on the menu. Somebody just has to work it out first.

shots.narration: Doug cruised along with his mouth open, minding his own business and filtering plankton,
until the costume rolled over and Doug stopped minding anything.
The biggest fish in the ocean, and only a handful of orcas seem to know it's food.
The Law of the Tongue.
This is the closest any orca has come to treating people as anything other than background.
From around the eighteen forties until about nineteen thirty,
at Twofold Bay near Eden in New South Wales, Australia, a group of orcas worked with shore whalers.
The orcas herded baleen whales into the bay.
Then one of them would swim to the mouth of the Kiah River, where the whalers lived,
and slap the water with its tail to call the boats out.
The best known of them, a male called Old Tom,
would sometimes grab a boat's rope in his teeth and tow it.
The rope wear is still visible on his teeth.
In return, the whalers kept what became known as the law of the tongue.
They left the catch in the water overnight, and the orcas took the tongue and lips.
The arrangement lasted roughly ninety years,
long enough for three generations of one whaling family, the Davidsons.
Old Tom was found dead in the bay in September nineteen thirty, and the whalers preserved his skeleton.
And this is the important part.
Orcas have hunted alongside people before,
and for close to a century, they treated us as partners, not prey.
The last time Doug met orcas in a boat, they took the rudder.
This time, one took his rope in its teeth and towed him.
Doug is fine.
Old Tom's skeleton is still on display at the Eden Killer Whale Museum, rope marks and all.
Blue Whale.
This is the largest animal that has ever lived, and there is nothing bigger left to hunt.
A blue whale can weigh up to about one hundred and fifty tonnes,

shots.narration: the same as roughly seventy-five average new cars, or nearly nineteen hundred Dougs.
Off southwestern Australia, researchers recorded orcas killing blue whales three times
between two thousand nineteen and two thousand twenty-one.
The first was a healthy adult, two weeks later came a calf, and in two thousand twenty-one, a juvenile.
When the researchers reached the first hunt, around fourteen orcas were attacking, with females leading.
Around fifty orcas ended up in the area, sharing the meal.
At least sixteen of the same orcas took part in all three hunts.
The researchers saw the orcas go for the tongue first, the same share the whalers of Eden used to leave them.
So here is the last clue.
It isn't size, because they'll take the largest animal that has ever lived.

shots.narration: It isn't danger, because venomous rays and great whites don't stop them.

shots.narration: And it isn't hunger, because some of them would rather go hungry than change the menu.

shots.narration: The leading explanation is about families.
United States government scientists say each orca population's diet is driven mainly by hunting tactics that are learned.
The researcher Erich Hoyt calls orcas fussy eaters,
very conservative about whatever they learned from their mothers and their pod.
And no one has ever recorded an orca family teaching its young to hunt people.
Doug wore the biggest costume we have ever made,
so big that only the cap stuck out of the blowhole, and then the orcas arrived.
Doug has died. Again.
Later, Doug went back out in a tiny boat, with no costume at all.
An orca surfaced, looked at him and swam off,
then came back and dropped a fish into his boat.
That part is real.
A study published in two thousand twenty-five collected thirty-four cases
from the past two decades of wild orcas offering food to people,
from California to New Zealand, Norway and Patagonia.
In all but one, the orcas waited to see what the people would do.
They hunt everything in the ocean.
